dispositions.rationale: Agreed: §1941.3(b) notice is limited to deficiencies covered by subsection (a). Reviewer's wording adopted in substance, in plainer second person for the Quick Answer; script wording adopted verbatim.
dispositions.change_applied: Quick Answer final two sentences replaced; fourth paragraph of the Video Script replaced in 10195 and 10196 (and the HeyGen script in the package notes).
dispositions.quote_before: Then respond to every security report quickly and keep a record. A report is notice under Civil Code §1941.3, and what you do after notice is what courts look at.
dispositions.quote_after: Then acknowledge every security report quickly, assess it and keep a record. A report of a broken lock or other deficiency covered by Civil Code §1941.3 can put you on notice, and the statute allows a reasonable time to fix it. Other security reports can raise duties under other law, so assess and document each one.

dispositions.rationale: Agreed: §1946.8(b)-(c) protect calls made by or on behalf of a person facing abuse, a crime or an emergency who believes help is necessary; the draft stated it unconditionally.
dispositions.change_applied: Key Facts row heading and text, words-table 'Why' cell, FAQ 4 question and answer, and the third Video Script paragraph (both posts) rewritten to carry the statute's conditions.
dispositions.quote_before: Tenants can always call the police | A lease term that limits a tenant's right to call law enforcement or emergency help is void.
dispositions.quote_after: Protected calls for police or emergency help | Civil Code §1946.8 protects calls made by or on behalf of someone facing abuse, a crime or an emergency who believes help is needed. A lease can't restrict those calls, and a landlord can't penalize a tenant or resident for them (fees, eviction, non-renewal or worse terms). No documentation is required to show that belief.

dispositions.quote_before: Step 5 is the one owners skip. A single incident is rarely foreseeable.
dispositions.quote_after: Step 5 is the one owners skip. Don't wait for a second incident before assessing a known hazard. The duty depends on how foreseeable the risk is and how burdensome the precaution would be, and hiring guards takes a higher level of foreseeability than simpler fixes.

dispositions.rationale: Agreed the 'leave out' list could read as advice to withhold known incidents, and the negative statutory claim was unsupported. Kept the C.A.R. neighborhood-conditions sentences that follow; replaced the list and the bulletin sentence.
dispositions.change_applied: 'What to leave out' sentences replaced; 'No statute requires a general crime bulletin. But' replaced.
dispositions.quote_before: What to leave out: crime statistics you've pulled together yourself, a description of the neighborhood, and any claim about how often something happens at the building. Stick to what to do and who to call.
dispositions.quote_after: What to leave out: unsupported safety ratings, crime statistics you've pulled together yourself, and promises about outcomes. That doesn't mean holding back known safety information. When you know about a specific incident or hazard, get legal advice about whether to warn or disclose.
